2.note: The author is using the adjectives **firstborn**, **second**, **third**, and **fourth** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases, here and in verses 3–5 and 10–11. Alternate translation: [the eldest son … son number two … son number three … son number four]

5.note: Here the word **for** introduces not a reason but an observation. Alternate translation: [indeed,]

6.note: The expression **were born** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And Shemaiah his son had sons]

6.q: הַ⁠מִּמְשָׁלִ֖ים לְ⁠בֵ֣ית אֲבִי⁠הֶ֑ם כִּֽי־גִבּ֥וֹרֵי חַ֖יִל הֵֽמָּה
6.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [and since they were warriors of valor, they were rulers in the house of their father]

9.note: See how you translated the expression “sons and brothers” in 25:10–31. Alternate translation: [And sons and other relatives]

10.note: See how you translated the term “head” in 23:8. Alternate translation: [the leader … the leader]

12.note: See how you translated the same expression in 24:4. Alternate translation: [to the clan leaders]
The author is using the term **brothers** to mean “relatives.” Alternate translation: [their kinsmen] or [their fellow Levites]
See how you translated the same expression in 25:6. Alternate translation: [in the temple of Yahweh]

13.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 25:8. Alternate translation: [for each clan, without regard to how important it was]

The author is using **for gate and gate** as a common expression of his culture to mean “for each gate.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for each gate] or [to assign the gates]

14.note: When the author says that this lot **fell to Shemeliah**, he is using a common expression of his culture to mean that when the leaders cast this lot, the result indicated Shemeliah. He does not mean that this lot literally fell onto Shemeliah. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the eastward lot came up for Shelemiah] or [And the eastward lot selected Shelemiah]

The author is describing this lot as **eastward** to mean that it was the one that would assign the eastward gate of the temple courtyard to a group of Levites to guard. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language, hear and for the terms **northward** in this verse and “southward” in the next verse. Alternate translation: [the lot for the eastward gate]

The name **Shemeliah** is a variant of the name “Meshelemiah” in verse 1. Recall whether your translation team decided to use the same name for a given person in each instance where he appears or whether you decided to use the name that the biblical author does, even if that is a variant. Alternate translation: [to Meshelemiah]

14.q: וּ⁠זְכַרְיָ֨הוּ בְנ֜⁠וֹ יוֹעֵ֣ץ ׀ בְּ⁠שֶׂ֗כֶל הִפִּ֨ילוּ֙ גּֽוֹרָל֔וֹת וַ⁠יֵּצֵ֥א גוֹרָל֖⁠וֹ צָפֽוֹנָ⁠ה
14.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about which gate this lot selected before the information about who Zechariah was. Alternate translation: [And the lot for the northward gate, when they cast it, came out for Zechariah his son, who was a counselor with insight]

15.q: לְ⁠עֹבֵ֥ד אֱדֹ֖ם נֶ֑גְבָּ⁠ה וּ⁠לְ⁠בָנָ֖י⁠ו בֵּ֥ית הָ⁠אֲסֻפִּֽים
15.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [When the lot for Obed Edom came out, it indicated that he and his group would guard the southward gate, and when the lot for his sons came out, it indicated that they would guard the house of stores]

The author is using this possessive form to describe a **house** (that is, a building, an annex of the temple) that was characterized by being a place where **stores** (that is, supplies and equipment) were kept. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the storehouse]

16.q: לְ⁠שֻׁפִּ֤ים וּ⁠לְ⁠חֹסָה֙ לַֽ⁠מַּעֲרָ֔ב עִ֚ם שַׁ֣עַר שַׁלֶּ֔כֶת בַּֽ⁠מְסִלָּ֖ה הָ⁠עוֹלָ֑ה
16.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [When the lots for Shuppim and Hosah came out, they indicated that they and their groups would guard the western gate and the gate of Shallecheth on the ascending highway]

The author seems to be using this phrase to indicate that while these two gates were close together, each had its own guards. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [with each gate having its own guards]

17.note: The author is representing each of these gates by referring to from what direction a person would enter through them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [At the eastern gate … at the northern gate … at the southern gate]

It seems that **six Levites** were needed as gatekeepers at the eastern gate, as opposed to **four** at the other gates, because the eastern gate was the main entrance to the temple courtyard, and so it was the busiest. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [At the busy eastern gate]

In the ancient Greek translation, the phrase “to the day” follows this phrase, as in the rest of the verse. This seems to be the original reading. You may want to follow that reading, or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [six Levites to the day]

The author is using **to the day** as a common expression of his culture to mean “each day.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [per day … per day] or [each day … each day]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [two at each of the two entrances]

19.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 6:33. Alternate translation: [for the clan of the Korahites and for the clan of the Merarites]

20.note: The word **Ahijah** is a translation of the standard Hebrew text as we have it today. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. No one named Ahijah appears in the preceding lists of Levites, and this chapter describes Shebuel and Shelemoth as responsible for the two types of treasuries. You may want to follow an alternative reading from the ancient Greek translation, which involves a difference of only one letter, or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [And the Levites, their brothers, were over] or [And their fellow Levites were over]

The author is using the adjective **holy** as a noun to mean a certain kind of thing. The ULT indicates this by supplying the word **things**. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase, here and in verses 26 and 28. Alternate translation: [the gifts people had dedicated] or [the votive offerings]

21.note: The term “sons” is literal in most of this chapter, but here, in the first instance, **sons** means “descendants,” and in the second instance, it means “clan members.” For the second instance, see how you translated the similar expressions in verse 19. Alternate translation: [The descendants of Ladan, the members of the clan of the Gershonites who were descendants of Ladan]

21.q: בְּנֵ֣י לַ֠עְדָּן בְּנֵ֨י הַ⁠גֵּרְשֻׁנִּ֜י לְ⁠לַעְדָּ֗ן רָאשֵׁ֧י הָ⁠אָב֛וֹת לְ⁠לַעְדָּ֥ן הַ⁠גֵּרְשֻׁנִּ֖י יְחִיאֵלִֽי
21.note: It might seem that this verse contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [The leaders of the clan of the Gershonites who were descendants of Ladan included Jehieli] or [Jehieli was one of the leaders of the clan of the Gershonites who were descendants of Ladan]

24.note: In the first instance, **son** means “descendant,” while in the second instance, **son** is literal. Alternate translation: [Shebuel, a descendant of Gershom, the son of Moses]

25.q: וְ⁠אֶחָ֖י⁠ו לֶֽ⁠אֱלִיעֶ֑זֶר רְחַבְיָ֨הוּ בְנ֜⁠וֹ וִֽ⁠ישַׁעְיָ֤הוּ בְנ⁠וֹ֙
25.note: The pronoun **his** refers in the first instance to Shebuel, while in the subsequent instances in this verse, the pronoun **his** refers to the preceding descendant of Eliezer. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Shebuel’s brothers who were to Eliezer: Rehabiah, Eliezer’s son, and Jeshaiah, Rehabiah’s son]
Here and in verses 26, 28, 30, and 32, the author is using the term **brothers** to mean “relatives.” Alternate translation: [And his kinsmen] or [And his fellow Levites]

26.note: The author seems to be saying **He, Shelemoth** to make clear that **He … and his brothers** does not refer back to Shebuel, as “his brothers” does in the previous verse. He may also wish to distinguish this **Shelomoth** from other Levites with the same name or a very similar name whom he has mentioned previously. It might seem that this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [Shelomoth and his brothers]

26.q: אֲשֶׁ֨ר הִקְדִּ֜ישׁ דָּוִ֣יד הַ⁠מֶּ֗לֶךְ וְ⁠רָאשֵׁ֧י הָ⁠אָב֛וֹת לְ⁠שָׂרֵֽי־הָ⁠אֲלָפִ֥ים וְ⁠הַ⁠מֵּא֖וֹת וְ⁠שָׂרֵ֥י הַ⁠צָּבָֽא
26.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put all the information together about who **consecrated** these holy things. Alternate translation: [that King David and the heads of fathers who were commanders of thousands and hundreds and commanders of the army consecrated]

27.note: The words **battles** and **plunder** together express a single idea. The word **battles** tells how the Israelites got this **plunder**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [From battle plunder] or [From plunder from battles]

28.q: וְ⁠כֹ֨ל הַֽ⁠הִקְדִּ֜ישׁ שְׁמוּאֵ֤ל הָ⁠רֹאֶה֙ וְ⁠שָׁא֣וּל בֶּן־קִ֔ישׁ וְ⁠אַבְנֵ֣ר בֶּן־נֵ֔ר וְ⁠יוֹאָ֖ב בֶּן־צְרוּיָ֑ה
28.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put all the information together about who **consecrated** these holy things. Alternate translation: [And everything Samuel the seer, Saul son of Kish, Abner son of Ner, and Joab son of Zeruiah consecrated]
See how you translated the similar expression in 19:11. Alternate translation: [were under the control of] or [were the responsibility of]

29.q: לַ⁠יִּצְהָרִ֞י כְּנַנְיָ֣הוּ וּ⁠בָנָ֗י⁠ו לַ⁠מְּלָאכָ֤ה הַ⁠חִֽיצוֹנָה֙ עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל לְ⁠שֹׁטְרִ֖ים וּ⁠לְ⁠שֹׁפְטִֽים
29.note: Since this is a heading that introduces a third major responsibility of the Levites described in this chapter, you may want to put the information about this **work** before the information about who did it. Alternate translation: [The outside work for Israel as officials and judges was done, from the Izharites, by Chenaniah and his sons]

The author is not referring to a specific **Isharite**. He means the Izharites in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language, here and for the similar expressions in verses 30, 31, and 32. Alternate translation: [From the Izharites]

30.note: The author is using the expression **sons of** to indicate that these men had the characteristic of something. In this case, these men were characterized by their **valor** or capability and exemplary character. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly, here and in verse 32 and for the equivalent expression “men of valor” in verse 31. Alternate translation: [capable men] or [responsible men]

31.note: See how you translated the same expression in 24:4. Alternate translation: [a clan leader of the Hebronites]
See how you translated the term “generations” in 5:7 and [7:1](ta:07). Alternate translation: [as the genealogy of his ancestors indicated]

31.q: בִּ⁠שְׁנַ֨ת הָֽ⁠אַרְבָּעִ֜ים לְ⁠מַלְכ֤וּת דָּוִיד֙ נִדְרָ֔שׁוּ וַ⁠יִּמָּצֵ֥א בָ⁠הֶ֛ם גִּבּ֥וֹרֵי חַ֖יִל בְּ⁠יַעְזֵ֥יר גִּלְעָֽד
31.note: The author is providing background information to explain how David’s officials found members of the Hebronite clan who could serve as officials and judges east of the Jordan River, just as members of that clan were already serving west of that river. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **40** in a context such as this, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [In the fortieth year of the reign of David]

The expressions **were sought** and **was found** are a passive verbal forms. If your language would not use those forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [his officials sought them, and they found men of valor among them]

The pronouns **they** and **them** refer to Hebronites, whom David and his officials were hoping to find in the Israelite territory east of the Jordan River. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [his officials sought Hebronites, and they found men of valor who were Hebronites]
